connections.label: The Sabbath rests on the seventh day of creation
connections.explanation: Exodus 20:8–11 recalls Genesis 2:1–3: the Sabbath commandment gives as its reason the six days of making and God's rest on the seventh. Genesis says God finished his work, rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy. The commandment says the LORD made heaven and earth in six days and rested, and therefore blessed the Sabbath and made it holy, with the same Hebrew word for the seventh day (below).

ends.excerpt: The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished. On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work,

connections.label: The kings of Edom, listed twice
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 1:43–54 retells Genesis 36:31–43: the kings who reigned in Edom before Israel had a king, and the chiefs of Esau, name by name. The list opens with the same words in both books and runs through the same kings and cities, beginning with Bela son of Beor at Dinhabah, almost line for line. Rare names such as Dinhabah and Masrekah occur only in these two passages (below).

ends.excerpt: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel.

ends.sectionTitle: Genealogies: From Adam to the Kings of Edom
ends.excerpt: Now these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel: Bela the son of Beor; and the name of his city was Dinhabah.

connections.label: Two blessings on Joseph
connections.explanation: Genesis 49:22–26 and Deuteronomy 33:13–17 both tell of a dying leader's blessing on Joseph, Jacob's and then Moses', in shared words. Both call down blessings of the heavens and of the deep that lies beneath, and both end on the same line: on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the one set apart from his brothers. The Hebrew words for the crown of the head and for the one set apart are shared (below); which blessing was written first is not stated.

ends.sectionTitle: Jacob's Blessings and Death; Joseph's Last Days
ends.excerpt: “Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a spring. His branches run over the wall. The archers have severely grieved him, shot at him, and persecuted him:
About Joseph he said, “His land is blessed by the LORD, for the precious things of the heavens, for the dew, for the deep that couches beneath,

connections.label: Is anything too hard for the LORD?
connections.explanation: Genesis 18:14 and Jeremiah 32:17–27 both tell that nothing is too hard for the LORD, once as his question to Abraham and once in Jeremiah's prayer and God's reply. In Genesis the LORD asks it when Sarah laughs at the promise of a son in her old age. In Jeremiah the prophet confesses it after buying a field, and the LORD answers with the same question; the Hebrew verb for being too hard is the same (below).

ends.excerpt: Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes around, and Sarah will have a son.”
“Ah Lord GOD! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm. There is nothing too hard for you.

connections.label: Joseph's story sung
connections.explanation: Psalms 105:16–22 retells Genesis 37:2–41:57: Joseph sold as a slave, his feet in shackles, freed by the king and made ruler of his house. The psalm names Joseph and follows the story step by step: a famine, a man sent ahead, the word that proved him true, the king who set him free and put him over all his possessions. It tells each step as the LORD's own act: he called the famine and he sent the man.

ends.excerpt: This is the history of the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives.…
He called for a famine on the land. He destroyed the food supplies. He sent a man before them. Joseph was sold for a slave.

connections.label: Blessed who blesses, cursed who curses
connections.explanation: Genesis 12:3 and Numbers 24:9 both tell that whoever blesses is blessed and whoever curses is cursed, first in God's promise to Abram and then in Balaam's oracle over Israel. Balaam, brought to curse Israel, ends his third oracle on the same pairing of blessing and curse. The Hebrew verb for cursing is the same in both (below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Call and Wanderings of Abram
ends.excerpt: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
He couched, he lay down as a lion, as a lioness; who shall rouse him up? Everyone who blesses you is blessed. Everyone who curses you is cursed.”

connections.label: Abram called out of Ur
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:7–8 recalls Genesis 11:31–12:3: the great prayer of Nehemiah 9 confesses the LORD who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees. Genesis tells of Terah leaving Ur with Abram and of the LORD's call to leave country and kindred for the land he would show. The prayer gathers this, the new name Abraham and the covenant to give the land into one confession; Ur of the Chaldees is named in both (below).

ends.excerpt: Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram’s wife. They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to…
You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, gave him the name of Abraham,

connections.label: Moriah
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 3:1 names the place of Genesis 22:2: Solomon builds the LORD's house on Mount Moriah. Genesis sends Abraham to the land of Moriah to offer Isaac on one of its mountains; Chronicles places the temple on Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor where the LORD appeared to David. Moriah is named in these two verses alone (below), and Chronicles does not mention Abraham, so the link is the place itself.

ends.excerpt: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

Then Solomon began to build the LORD’s house at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David his father, which he prepared in the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor…

connections.label: A priest in the order of Melchizedek
connections.explanation: Psalms 110:4 names Melchizedek of Genesis 14:18–20: the LORD swears that the psalm's king is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses, as king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brings bread and wine and blesses Abram. Outside Genesis, the Old Testament names him only in this psalm (below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Call and Wanderings of Abram
ends.excerpt: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High. He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth.
The LORD has sworn, and will not change his mind: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.”

connections.label: As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah
connections.explanation: Amos 4:11 names the overthrow of Genesis 19:24–25: some of Israel were overthrown as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis tells how the LORD rained sulfur and fire on the two cities and overthrew them and all the plain. Amos uses the same verb for overthrowing (below), in a list of judgements after each of which Israel still did not return.

ends.excerpt: Then the LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of the sky.
“I have overthrown some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a burning stick plucked out of the fire; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says the LORD.

connections.label: Rulers of Sodom, people of Gomorrah
connections.explanation: Isaiah 1:9–10 names the cities of Genesis 19:24–25: only a small remnant kept Judah from becoming like Sodom and Gomorrah, and its rulers are then addressed as rulers of Sodom. Genesis tells of the two cities overthrown by fire. Isaiah turns their names first into a measure of near destruction and then into a charge against Jerusalem's leaders and people (the names below).

ends.excerpt: Then the LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of the sky.
Unless the LORD of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom. We would have been like Gomorrah.

connections.label: Jacob took his brother by the heel
connections.explanation: Hosea 12:3 recalls Genesis 25:26: in the womb Jacob took his brother by the heel. Genesis tells it at the twins' birth, the second child coming out with his hand on Esau's heel and being named Jacob. Hosea recalls it in a charge against Jacob's descendants, setting their ancestor's grasping at birth beside his struggle with God.

ends.excerpt: After that, his brother came out, and his hand had hold on Esau’s heel. He was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he contended with God. Indeed, he struggled with the angel, and prevailed; he wept, and made supplication to him. He found him at…

connections.label: Jacob struggled with God and prevailed
connections.explanation: Hosea 12:3–4 recalls Genesis 32:24–30: in his manhood Jacob contended with God; he struggled with the angel and prevailed. Genesis tells of the night Jacob wrestled a man until daybreak, would not let him go without a blessing and was given the name Israel. Hosea adds that he wept and pleaded, and the verb for his struggling (below) occurs only in these two passages.

ends.excerpt: Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day. When he saw that he didn’t prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob’s…
In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he contended with God. Indeed, he struggled with the angel, and prevailed; he wept, and made supplication to him. He found him at…

connections.label: The waters of Noah
connections.explanation: Isaiah 54:9 recalls Genesis 9:11–15: as God swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth, so he swears not to be angry with Zion. Genesis tells of the covenant after the flood, sealed with the rainbow in the cloud. Isaiah takes that oath as the pattern for God's own oath to his people.

ends.excerpt: I will establish my covenant with you: All flesh will not be cut off any more by the waters of the flood. There will never again be a flood to destroy the earth.”
“For this is like the waters of Noah to me; for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah will no more go over the earth, so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you, nor rebuke you.

connections.label: Look to Abraham
connections.explanation: Isaiah 51:2 recalls Genesis 12:1–3: Zion is told to look to Abraham and Sarah, for God called Abraham when he was one man, blessed him and made him many. Genesis tells of the call to leave country and kindred and the promise of a great nation and a blessing. Isaiah offers that beginning as a reason to trust that God can do the same again.

ends.sectionTitle: The Call and Wanderings of Abram
ends.excerpt: Now the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, I blessed him, and made him many.

connections.label: Jacob loved, Esau hated
connections.explanation: Malachi 1:2–3 recalls Genesis 25:23–34: Esau was Jacob's brother, yet the LORD loved Jacob and hated Esau. Genesis tells of the word to Rebekah that two nations were in her womb and the elder would serve the younger, and of Esau selling his birthright. Malachi answers Israel's question of how God has loved them by pointing to that choice and to the desolation of Esau's mountains.

ends.excerpt: The LORD said to her, “Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be separated from your body. The one people will be stronger than the other people. The elder will serve the younger.”

connections.label: Rachel's tomb
connections.explanation: 1 Samuel 10:2 names the grave of Genesis 35:19–20: Samuel tells Saul he will meet two men by Rachel's tomb, on the border of Benjamin. Genesis tells of Rachel dying on the way to Ephrath and of Jacob setting up a pillar on her grave that stood to the writer's day. Samuel uses the tomb as a landmark on Saul's road home, with the same Hebrew word for the grave (below).

ends.excerpt: Rachel died, and was buried on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem). Jacob set up a pillar on her grave. The same is the Pillar of Rachel’s grave to this day.
When you have departed from me today, then you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb, on the border of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys which you went to look for have been found…

connections.label: The house of Perez
connections.explanation: Ruth 4:12 names the birth of Genesis 38:27–30: the elders bless Boaz's house to be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah. Genesis tells of the twins born to Tamar, the second breaking out first and named Perez. The book of Ruth ends with the line from Perez to David, so the blessing points to the family Ruth is joining (the name below).

ends.excerpt: In the time of her travail, behold, twins were in her womb. When she travailed, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, “This came out first.”
Let your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, of the offspring which the LORD will give you by this young woman.”

connections.label: Joshua tells the story from Terah
connections.explanation: Joshua 24:2–4 retells Genesis 11:26–12:5: Terah beyond the River, Abraham taken from there and led through Canaan, then Isaac, Jacob and Esau. At Shechem Joshua opens the covenant by telling the story of Genesis in the LORD's own voice, down to Jacob's family going down into Egypt. Genesis does not say that Terah served other gods; Joshua's retelling adds it.

ends.excerpt: Terah lived seventy years, and became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

Joshua said to all the people, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Your fathers lived of old time beyond the River, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor. They served other gods.

connections.label: Joseph's bones carried up
connections.explanation: Exodus 13:19 quotes Genesis 50:24–25: Moses takes Joseph's bones, because Joseph had made Israel swear that when God visited them they would carry his bones up. Exodus repeats Joseph's words almost exactly, so the oath sworn at his death is kept as Israel leaves Egypt. The Hebrew words for the visiting and for the bones are the same (below).

ends.sectionTitle: Jacob's Blessings and Death; Joseph's Last Days
ends.excerpt: Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”
Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for he had made the children of Israel swear, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones away from here with you.”

connections.label: The field at Shechem
connections.explanation: Joshua 24:32 recalls Genesis 33:19: Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem in the plot Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of money. Genesis tells of Jacob buying the ground where he had spread his tent; Joshua names the same field, the same sellers and the same price, and it becomes the inheritance of Joseph's children. The rare word for the pieces of money (below) occurs only three times in the Old Testament.

ends.excerpt: He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money.

connections.label: Formless and empty
connections.explanation: Genesis 1:2 and Jeremiah 4:23 both tell of the earth formless and empty, once before the first day and once in the prophet's vision of a land undone. Jeremiah adds that the heavens had no light, as before light was made. The second of the two Hebrew words occurs only three times in the Old Testament, twice here (below); which passage is the older is not stated.

ends.excerpt: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
I saw the earth and, behold, it was waste and void, and the heavens, and they had no light.

connections.label: In Eden, the garden of God
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 28:13 names the garden of Genesis 2:8–15: the king of Tyre was in Eden, the garden of God, adorned with precious stones. Genesis places the garden in Eden, watered by a river that runs toward a land of gold, bdellium and onyx. Ezekiel's lament gives Tyre's king that garden's splendour before his fall, and Eden and the onyx are named in both (below).

ends.excerpt: The LORD God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.

ends.sectionTitle: Lament for Tyre; the Prince of Tyre; Sidon
ends.excerpt: You were in Eden, the garden of God. Every precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, emerald, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and beryl. Gold work of tambourines and of pipes was in…

connections.label: A king's dream, and the God who explains it
connections.explanation: Genesis 41:1–40 and Daniel 2:1–49 both tell of a foreign king troubled by a dream, his magicians unable to explain it, and a Hebrew captive who credits God and is raised to high office. Pharaoh's spirit is troubled and so is Nebuchadnezzar's; Joseph says the answer belongs to God, and Daniel says there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets. The Hebrew words for the troubled spirit and for the magicians are shared (below).

ends.excerpt: At the end of two full years, Pharaoh dreamed, and behold, he stood by the river. Behold, seven cattle came up out of the river. They were sleek and fat, and they fed in the marsh grass.
In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him.

connections.label: Rule over the works of God's hands
connections.explanation: Genesis 1:26–28 and Psalms 8:4–8 both tell of humankind given rule over the creatures: the flocks and herds, the animals of the field, the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea. Genesis gives that rule at creation, with the image of God. The psalm marvels that God should care for so small a creature and has put all things under his feet.

ends.excerpt: God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over…
what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him? For you have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor.

connections.label: Noah, Daniel and Job
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 14:14 names Noah of Genesis 6:9: even Noah, Daniel and Job, were they in a guilty land, would save only themselves by their righteousness. Genesis calls Noah righteous and blameless among the people of his time. Ezekiel sets him beside two other righteous men to say that a land will not be spared for the sake of a few (the name below).

ends.excerpt: This is the history of the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.

ends.sectionTitle: The Exile Acted Out; False Prophets
ends.excerpt: though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness,” says the Lord GOD.

connections.label: The first Passover in the land
connections.explanation: Joshua 5:10–11 names the feast of Exodus 12:6: in Gilgal Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, as the law set it. Exodus fixes the lamb for the fourteenth day, killed at evening; Joshua records the first Passover kept in the land, on that day and at that hour, on the plains of Jericho. On the next day they eat the produce of the land.

ends.excerpt: You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.

ends.sectionTitle: Gilgal and the Commander of the Army
ends.excerpt: The children of Israel encamped in Gilgal. They kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening in the plains of Jericho.

connections.label: Jericho heard of the Red Sea
connections.explanation: Joshua 2:10 recalls Exodus 14:21–22: Rahab tells the spies that Jericho has heard of the LORD drying up the Red Sea before Israel. Exodus tells of the east wind that drove the sea back all night and made it dry ground. In Jericho the story has travelled ahead of Israel and is told back to them by a Canaanite woman.

ends.excerpt: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.

For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you, when you came out of Egypt; and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites, who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and to…

connections.label: The Jordan dried up as the Red Sea was
connections.explanation: Joshua 4:23 recalls Exodus 14:21–22: the LORD dried up the Jordan before Israel as he had dried up the Red Sea. Exodus tells of the sea driven back and Israel crossing on dry ground with the waters a wall on either side. Joshua makes the crossing of the Jordan its second telling, so that children who ask about the stones will hear of both.

ends.excerpt: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan from before you until you had crossed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up from before us, until we had crossed…

connections.label: The LORD is my strength and song
connections.explanation: Exodus 15:2 and Psalms 118:14 both tell that the LORD is my strength and song and has become my salvation, once in the Song of the Sea and once in a psalm of thanksgiving. The line is the same in the Hebrew, including a rare word for song (below), and Isaiah 12:2 has it too. Which was sung first is not stated.

ends.excerpt: The LORD is my strength and song. He has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will praise him; my father’s God, and I will exalt him.
The LORD is my strength and song. He has become my salvation. The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. “The right hand of the LORD does valiantly.

connections.label: The manna ceased
connections.explanation: Joshua 5:12 recalls Exodus 16:35: the manna ceased the day after Israel ate the produce of Canaan. Exodus says Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan. Joshua records the day it stopped, at Gilgal, and the word for the manna is the same (below).

ends.excerpt: The children of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan.

ends.sectionTitle: Gilgal and the Commander of the Army
ends.excerpt: The manna ceased on the next day, after they had eaten of the produce of the land. The children of Israel didn’t have manna any more, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.

connections.label: As at Meribah, as at Massah
connections.explanation: Psalms 95:8–9 names the places of Exodus 17:7: the psalm warns against a hardened heart like Israel's at Meribah and Massah. Exodus names the place Massah and Meribah because the people quarrelled and tested the LORD, asking whether he was among them or not. The psalm turns the two names back into what they mean, testing and quarrelling, as a warning to those who sing it (below).

ends.excerpt: He called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because the children of Israel quarreled, and because they tested the LORD, saying, “Is the LORD among us, or not?”
Don’t harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness, when your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my work.

connections.label: The Ten Commandments, given twice
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 5:6–21 retells Exodus 20:1–17: Moses repeats the Ten Commandments to the people about to enter the land. The commandments run in the same order with nearly the same words, and the Hebrew shares rare words such as those for the image and for coveting (below). Two differences stand out: Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath in Israel's slavery in Egypt, where Exodus grounds it in the six days of creation, and it names the neighbour's wife before his house.

ends.excerpt: God spoke all these words, saying, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

connections.label: The golden calf, remembered
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 9:8–21 retells Exodus 32:1–20: Moses reminds Israel of the calf they made at Horeb while he stayed forty days on the mountain. Both tell of the molten calf, the LORD's anger and his word to let him destroy them, the tablets broken, and the calf burnt and ground to dust; the Hebrew for the molten image and for the grinding is shared (below). Deuteronomy adds that Moses fasted forty days and nights and prayed for Aaron too.

ends.excerpt: When the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron, and said to him, “Come, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this…
Also in Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was angry with you to destroy you.

connections.label: A calf in Horeb
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:19–20 recalls Exodus 32:4: they made a calf in Horeb and worshipped a molten image. Exodus tells how Aaron fashioned the molten calf and the people hailed it as the gods who brought them out of Egypt. The psalm says that so they exchanged their glory for the image of a bull that eats grass, with the same words for the calf and the molten image (below).

ends.excerpt: He received what they handed him, fashioned it with an engraving tool, and made it a molded calf. Then they said, “These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.”
They made a calf in Horeb, and worshiped a molten image. Thus they exchanged their glory for an image of a bull that eats grass.

connections.label: Moses prays God's own words back
connections.explanation: Numbers 14:17–19 quotes Exodus 34:6–7: after the spies' report Moses prays back to God the words God proclaimed of himself, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness. Moses introduces them as what the LORD has spoken, keeps the line about forgiving iniquity and visiting it to the third and fourth generation, and asks pardon by the greatness of that loving kindness. The Hebrew for slow to anger and for clearing the guilty is the same (below).

ends.excerpt: The LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
Now please let the power of the Lord be great, according as you have spoken, saying, ‘The LORD is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, forgiving iniquity and disobedience; and he will by…

connections.label: Merciful and gracious, slow to anger
connections.explanation: Exodus 34:6 and Jonah 4:2 both tell of a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness, once proclaimed at Sinai and once thrown back at God by an angry prophet. Jonah says he fled to Tarshish because he knew God was like this and would relent of doing harm. The Hebrew words for merciful and gracious are the same (below); which passage is the older is not stated.

ends.excerpt: The LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
He prayed to the LORD, and said, “Please, LORD, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God and…

connections.label: The cloud fills the dwelling
connections.explanation: Exodus 40:34–35 and 1 Kings 8:10–11 both tell of the cloud filling God's dwelling once it is finished, so that no one can go in. At the tabernacle Moses cannot enter because the cloud rests on it and the LORD's glory fills it; at the temple the priests cannot stand to minister because of the cloud, for the LORD's glory fills the house. The Hebrew words for the cloud and the glory are the same (below).

ends.excerpt: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the LORD’s glory filled the tabernacle. Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud stayed on it, and the LORD’s glory…
It came to pass, when the priests had come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled the LORD’s house,

connections.label: Him who lived in the bush
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 33:16 names the bush of Exodus 3:2–4: Moses blesses Joseph with the good will of him who lived in the bush. Exodus tells of the bush that burned and was not consumed, from which God called Moses. In his last blessing Moses names the LORD by that meeting, and the Hebrew word for this bush occurs only in these two passages (below).

ends.excerpt: The LORD’s angel appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the middle of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
for the precious things of the earth and its fullness, the good will of him who lived in the bush. Let this come on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the head of him who was separated from his…

connections.label: May his face shine on us
connections.explanation: Numbers 6:24–26 and Psalms 67:1 both tell of a prayer that God will bless and make his face shine, in the priests' blessing and in a psalm's opening. The psalm turns the blessing into the people's own request and goes on to ask that God's way be known on earth. The Hebrew words for shining and for being gracious are the same (below).

connections.label: Caleb remembers Kadesh Barnea
connections.explanation: Joshua 14:6–12 recalls Numbers 13:30–14:24: Caleb reminds Joshua of what the LORD said at Kadesh Barnea when the spies came back. Numbers tells of the twelve sent out, the frightened report of the many, Caleb's word that they could take the land, and the LORD's promise that Caleb, who followed him fully, would enter it. Forty-five years later Caleb, still strong, asks for the hill country that promise gave him.

connections.explanation: Psalms 106:16–18 recalls Numbers 16:31–33: the earth opened for Dathan and Abiram, who had envied Moses and Aaron. Numbers tells of the ground splitting under Korah's men and their households, who went down alive to Sheol. The psalm names Dathan and Abiram and the fire that burned the wicked, in its long confession of Israel's sins, with the same verb for swallowing (below).

connections.label: Moses at the waters of Meribah
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:32–33 recalls Numbers 20:10–13: at the waters of Meribah Moses was troubled for Israel's sake and spoke rashly. Numbers tells of Moses striking the rock twice and of the LORD's word that, because he did not believe or honour him, he would not lead the people into the land. The psalm lays the cause on the people's rebellion, which made Moses speak rashly with his lips (the place's name below).

connections.label: The bronze serpent broken
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 18:4 names the serpent of Numbers 21:8–9: Hezekiah broke in pieces the bronze serpent Moses had made, because Israel burned incense to it. Numbers tells how Moses set a bronze serpent on a pole so that whoever was bitten and looked at it lived. Kings records its end long after, when it had become an object of worship called Nehushtan, with the same words for serpent and bronze (below).

connections.label: Balaam sent for to curse
connections.explanation: Joshua 24:9–10 recalls Numbers 22:5–6: Balak king of Moab sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel, but the LORD would not listen to Balaam. Numbers tells of the messengers sent to Pethor by the River and of Balak's plea for a curse on a people too mighty for him. In Joshua's covenant speech the LORD tells the outcome in a line, that Balaam blessed Israel instead (the names below).

connections.label: Remember what Balak devised
connections.explanation: Micah 6:5 recalls Numbers 22:5–6: Israel is told to remember what Balak devised and what Balaam son of Beor answered him. Numbers tells of the king of Moab sending for the seer to curse a people too mighty for him. Micah sets the story among the LORD's righteous acts, in his case against his own people (the names below).

connections.label: Phinehas stood up
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:28–31 recalls Numbers 25:7–13: when Israel joined Baal Peor and a plague broke out, Phinehas stood up and the plague was stopped. Numbers tells of Phinehas's spear and of the covenant of a lasting priesthood given him for his zeal. The psalm says the act was credited to him as righteousness for all generations, and names him with the same word for the plague (below).

connections.label: Birds for the craving
connections.explanation: Psalms 78:26–31 retells Numbers 11:31–34: God sent a wind that brought birds down around the camp, and while the food was still in their mouths his anger struck them. Numbers tells of the quail let fall around the camp and gathered for two days, and of the plague that named the place for the graves of those who craved. The psalm keeps the order and makes it a lesson about desire that was granted and then judged.

connections.label: Moses laid his hands on Joshua
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 34:9 recalls Numbers 27:18–23: Joshua, on whom Moses had laid his hands, is filled with wisdom and Israel listens to him. Numbers tells of the LORD's command to take Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, lay a hand on him and commission him before Eleazar and the congregation so that Israel would obey him. At Moses' death Deuteronomy records that it was so, with the same verb for laying on hands (below).

connections.label: The cities of refuge
connections.explanation: Joshua 20:1–3 recalls Numbers 35:9–15: the LORD tells Joshua to assign the cities of refuge of which he spoke by Moses. Numbers sets out cities to which one who killed a person unintentionally could flee from the avenger until judged. Joshua repeats the law's terms, the unwitting killer and the avenger of blood, and then names the cities (the words below).

connections.label: The eastern tribes held to their word
connections.explanation: Joshua 1:12–15 recalls Numbers 32:20–22: Joshua reminds Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh of the word Moses commanded them. In Numbers they ask to settle east of the Jordan, and Moses agrees on condition that their armed men cross over and fight until the land is subdued. Before the crossing Joshua holds them to it.

connections.label: With all his heart, soul and might
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 23:25 recalls Deuteronomy 6:4–5: Josiah turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul and might, according to all the law of Moses. Deuteronomy commands Israel to love the LORD with heart, soul and might; Kings gives Josiah the same three, and says no king before or after was like him. The full three-part phrase, ending with might, occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament.

connections.label: A king like all the nations
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 17:14–15 and 1 Samuel 8:5 both tell of Israel asking for a king like all the nations around. Deuteronomy foresees the request and allows a king of the LORD's choosing, one of their own brothers. In Samuel the elders make the request, and the LORD tells Samuel that it is he they have rejected.

connections.label: Each shall die for his own sin
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 14:6 quotes Deuteronomy 24:16: Amaziah spared the children of his father's murderers, as written in the book of the law of Moses. Kings gives the law in full, that fathers shall not die for their children nor children for their fathers, but each for his own sin. It names the book of the law of Moses as its source (the word for sin below).

connections.explanation: Nehemiah 13:1–2 quotes Deuteronomy 23:3–5: the book of Moses, read to the people, says no Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of God. Deuteronomy gives the reasons, that they did not meet Israel with bread and water and hired Balaam to curse them, and adds that God turned the curse into a blessing. Nehemiah repeats all three, with the same Hebrew words (below), and the people separate from those of foreign descent.

connections.explanation: Daniel 9:11–13 names the curse of Deuteronomy 28:15–68: Daniel confesses that the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses have been poured out on Israel. Deuteronomy sets out the curses that will overtake Israel if it does not listen to the LORD's voice. Daniel's prayer confesses that this has happened, the great evil that came on Jerusalem coming as Moses wrote.

connections.explanation: Nehemiah 1:8–9 quotes Deuteronomy 30:1–4: Nehemiah asks God to remember his word to Moses, to scatter Israel if they sinned and to gather them if they returned. Deuteronomy promises that if the scattered return to the LORD with all their heart he will gather them even from the farthest parts of heaven. Nehemiah prays it back in the words of the promise (below), ending at the place God chose for his name.

connections.label: Be strong and courageous
connections.explanation: Joshua 1:5–9 echoes Deuteronomy 31:6–8: the LORD tells Joshua what Moses had told him, to be strong and courageous, for God will not fail or forsake him. In Deuteronomy Moses charges Joshua before all Israel. In Joshua the LORD repeats the charge after Moses' death and adds that he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses, in the same Hebrew words (below).

connections.label: Admah and Zeboiim
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 29:23 and Hosea 11:8 both tell of Admah and Zeboiim, cities overthrown with Sodom and Gomorrah. Deuteronomy holds up their overthrow as what a faithless land will become; Hosea has God ask how he can make Ephraim like them, and his compassion is stirred. The two names are rare (below); which passage is the older is not stated.

connections.label: The place he chooses for his name
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 12:5 and 1 Kings 8:29 both tell of the place the LORD chooses for his name. Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God will choose out of all their tribes to put his name there. At the temple's dedication Solomon prays toward the house of which God said that his name would be there.

connections.label: Jericho rebuilt at a cost
connections.explanation: 1 Kings 16:34 shows Joshua 6:26 fulfilled: Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho at the cost of his firstborn and his youngest son, according to the LORD's word spoken by Joshua. Joshua laid a curse on whoever rebuilt the city, that he would lose his firstborn when he laid its foundation and his youngest son when he hung its gates. Kings records it in the same terms, naming the sons Abiram and Segub, with the same words for foundation and youngest (below).

connections.label: The valley of Achor, a door of hope
connections.explanation: Hosea 2:15 names the valley of Joshua 7:24–26: God will make the valley of Achor a door of hope. Joshua tells how Achan, who took the devoted things, was stoned in that valley, named for the trouble he brought on Israel. Hosea promises that the place of that trouble will become an entrance to hope, as in the day Israel came up out of Egypt (the name below).

connections.label: Achar, the troubler of Israel
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 2:7 names Achan of Joshua 7:1: in Judah's genealogy the son of Carmi is Achar, the troubler of Israel, who trespassed in the devoted thing. Joshua names him Achan son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah, who took some of the devoted things. Chronicles spells his name to match the trouble he caused and keeps only that deed, with the same words for Carmi and the trespass (below).

connections.explanation: Joshua 10:12–14 and Habakkuk 3:11 both tell of the sun and moon standing still in the sky at the LORD's battle. In Joshua it is the answer to Joshua's word at Gibeon, so that the day lasted until Israel had defeated its enemies. Habakkuk's prayer sees sun and moon halted at the light of God's arrows, with the same words for sun and moon (below).

connections.explanation: 2 Samuel 21:1–2 recalls Joshua 9:15–20: a three-year famine comes because Saul put the Gibeonites to death, though Israel had sworn to them. Joshua tells how the princes of Israel, deceived, swore an oath to let the Gibeonites live and kept it once the truth came out. Samuel explains that the Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites, protected by that oath.

connections.explanation: Joshua 21:43–45 and 1 Kings 8:56 both tell that not one of the LORD's good promises to Israel failed, once at the end of the conquest and once at the temple's dedication. Joshua says the LORD gave the land and rest all around, and every word came to pass. Solomon blesses the LORD for giving rest to his people, for not one word of his promise by Moses has failed, with the same verb for failing (below).

connections.explanation: Psalms 114:3–5 recalls Joshua 3:14–17: the sea saw and fled, the Jordan was driven back. Joshua tells of the waters of the Jordan standing up in a heap when the priests' feet touched them. The psalm sets the Jordan beside the sea of the exodus and asks them both what made them turn back.

ends.excerpt: When the people moved from their tents to pass over the Jordan, the priests who bore the ark of the covenant went before the people.

connections.explanation: Isaiah 10:26 recalls Judges 7:19–25: the LORD will strike Assyria as in the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb. Judges tells of Gideon's night attack with trumpets and torches, the rout of Midian and the death of its prince Oreb at the rock that bears his name. Isaiah makes it a pattern for God's judgement on Assyria, beside the rod lifted over the sea (the names below).

connections.explanation: Psalms 83:9–11 recalls Judges 7:19–25: the psalm asks God to make Israel's enemies like Oreb and Zeeb, princes of Midian. Judges tells of Midian's defeat and of the princes Oreb and Zeeb killed at the rock and the winepress named for them. The psalm prays for the same end to a new alliance gathered against Israel (the names below).

connections.explanation: Psalms 83:9–10 recalls Judges 4:15–21: do to them as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon. Judges tells how the LORD threw Sisera's chariots into confusion before Barak and how Sisera, fleeing on foot, died in Jael's tent. The psalm sets that victory beside Gideon's over Midian (the names below).

connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:26–28 retells Judges 2:11–19: Israel rebelled, God gave them into their enemies' hands, they cried out and he sent saviours, and again they did evil. Judges sets out the cycle at the start of the book, from serving the Baals to the judges raised up and the people turning back once each judge died. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 tells the same cycle in the same order as part of its confession, with the same word for their distress (below).

connections.explanation: Judges 9:8–15 and 2 Kings 14:9 both tell of a fable in which plants speak, told to put an overreaching ruler in his place. Jotham tells of the trees seeking a king and the bramble that accepts; Jehoash king of Israel answers Amaziah's challenge with a thistle in Lebanon that asks a cedar for his daughter. They are the two plant fables of the historical books, with the cedars of Lebanon in both (below).

connections.explanation: Hosea 9:9 recalls Judges 19:22–30: Israel has corrupted itself as in the days of Gibeah. Judges tells of the crime at Gibeah, the abuse and death of the Levite's concubine, which the Israelites said had no equal since the exodus. Hosea makes the days of Gibeah the measure of Israel's corruption in his own time.

connections.explanation: Judges 13:5 and 1 Samuel 1:11 both tell of a child given to God from birth, on whose head no razor shall come. The angel tells Samson's mother that her son will be a Nazirite from the womb; Hannah vows that if the LORD gives her a son, he will be the LORD's all his days, with the same promise about the razor. Ruth closes with these ten generations as the book's last word; Chronicles sets them inside the larger family of Judah. connections.explanation: Ruth 4:11 names the mothers of Genesis 29:31–30:24: the elders bless Ruth to be like Rachel and Leah, who both built the house of Israel. Genesis tells of the sons born to Leah and Rachel and their maids, the rivalry between the sisters, and the LORD who opened their wombs. Ruth's blessing joins the two rivals as the builders of one house (the names below).

Deuteronomy sets the shame of the sandal on a brother who refuses to raise up a name for his dead brother. connections.explanation: 1 Samuel 2:1–10 and Psalms 113:7–9 both tell of the LORD who lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to sit with princes. Hannah sings it when Samuel is born, after years of barrenness; the psalm adds that God gives the barren woman a home as a joyful mother of children. connections.label: Cyrus, who will say of Jerusalem: let it be built
connections.explanation: Isaiah 44:28 and Ezra 1:1–2 both tell of Cyrus as the one through whom Jerusalem and its temple will be built. Isaiah has the LORD call Cyrus his shepherd, who will say of Jerusalem that it shall be built and of the temple that its foundation shall be laid. Ezra records Cyrus's decree that the LORD has charged him to build him a house in Jerusalem.

ends.sectionTitle: Israel the Witness; Idols Mocked; Cyrus
ends.excerpt: who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure,’ even saying of Jerusalem, ‘She will be built;’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation will be laid.’”

connections.label: The peoples of the lands
connections.explanation: Ezra 9:1–2 recalls Deuteronomy 7:1–3: the leaders report that Israel has not kept itself apart from the peoples of the lands, the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites and others. Deuteronomy lists the nations of the land and forbids marrying with them. Ezra's report names the same peoples (below) and says the holy offspring have mixed with them.

ends.excerpt: When the LORD your God brings you into the land where you go to possess it, and casts out many nations before you—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite…

connections.label: The register of the returned, twice
connections.explanation: Ezra 2:1–70 and Nehemiah 7:6–73 both tell the list of those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, family by family and town by town. Nehemiah says he found the register of those who came up first and sets it out; the two lists match name for name, with small differences in some of the numbers (rare names below). Which book holds the earlier copy is not stated.

ends.sectionTitle: Cyrus's Decree and the First Return

connections.label: Booths, found written in the law
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 8:14–17 quotes Leviticus 23:39–43: the people find written in the law that Israel should live in booths during the feast of the seventh month. Leviticus commands the feast with branches of trees, as a memorial that Israel lived in booths after the exodus. Nehemiah tells how the people gathered branches, built booths on roofs and in courtyards, and kept the feast as they had not since Joshua's day (the shared words below).

ends.excerpt: “‘So on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the fruits of the land, you shall keep the feast of the LORD seven days. On the first day shall be a solemn rest, and on the…
They found written in the law how the LORD had commanded by Moses that the children of Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month;

connections.label: The sea divided, confessed
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:9–11 recalls Exodus 14:21–28: God divided the sea before Israel so that they passed through on dry ground, and threw their pursuers into the depths. Exodus tells of the east wind, the dry ground and the waters returning on Pharaoh's army. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 tells it with the same words for the dry ground and the dividing (below), the pursuers thrown like a stone into mighty waters.

ends.excerpt: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
“You saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heard their cry by the Red Sea, and showed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his servants, and against all the people of his land…

connections.label: Sihon and Og
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:22 recalls Numbers 21:21–35: Israel took the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan. Numbers tells of the two kings who would not let Israel pass and were defeated east of the Jordan. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 counts their lands among the kingdoms God gave (the names below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Bronze Serpent and the March East
ends.excerpt: Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying, “Let me pass through your land. We will not turn away into field or vineyard. We will not drink of the water of the wells. We will go by…

connections.label: Bread from heaven, confessed
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:15 recalls Exodus 16:4–15: God gave Israel bread from heaven for their hunger. Exodus tells of the LORD raining bread from heaven, the manna the people did not recognise. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 joins it to the water brought out of the rock and the command to go in and possess the land.

ends.excerpt: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law…
and gave them bread from the sky for their hunger, and brought water out of the rock for them for their thirst, and commanded them that they should go in to possess the land which you had sworn to…

connections.label: For he is good
connections.explanation: Psalms 136:1 and Ezra 3:10–11 both tell the same refrain of thanks: the LORD is good, and his loving kindness endures forever. Psalm 136 repeats the second half after every line of Israel's story. At the founding of the second temple the priests and Levites sing it to one another, the people shout, and some who had seen the first house weep.

ends.excerpt: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his loving kindness endures forever.
When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD’s temple, they set the priests in their vestments with trumpets, with the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to…

connections.label: Not good for the man to be alone
connections.explanation: Tobit 8:6 quotes Genesis 2:18: on his wedding night Tobias prays to the God who made Adam and gave him Eve, and repeats God's word that it is not good for the man to be alone. Genesis gives that word before the woman is made, as the reason for a helper comparable to the man. Tobias's prayer names Adam and Eve and asks God's mercy on his marriage to Sarah.

ends.excerpt: The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”
You made Adam, and gave him Eve his wife for a helper and support. From them came the seed of men. You said, it is not good that the man should be alone. Let’s make him a helper like him.

connections.label: Feasts turned into mourning
connections.explanation: Tobit 2:6 quotes Amos 8:10: at the feast of Pentecost, after finding a murdered kinsman in the street, Tobit remembers the prophecy of Amos that feasts will be turned into mourning. Amos speaks of feasts turned to mourning and songs to lamentation, as for an only son. Tobit names the prophet and applies the line as his own feast ends in tears.

ends.excerpt: I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will make you wear sackcloth on all your bodies, and baldness on every head. I will make it like the mourning for an…
and remembered the prophecy of Amos, as he said, “Your feasts will be turned into mourning, and all your mirth into lamentation.

connections.label: What Jonah said of Nineveh
connections.explanation: Tobit 14:4 names the prophecy of Jonah 3:4: dying, Tobit tells his son to go to Media, for he believes what Jonah the prophet said of Nineveh, that it will be overthrown. Jonah tells of the warning that Nineveh would be overthrown in forty days, and of the city's repentance. Tobit, living in Nineveh, trusts that the word will yet come true.

ends.excerpt: Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried out, and said, “In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!”
Go into Media, my child, for I surely believe all the things which Jonah the prophet spoke of Nineveh, that it will be overthrown, but in Media there will rather be peace for a season. Our kindred…

connections.label: Abraham found faithful when tested
connections.explanation: 1 Maccabees 2:52 recalls Genesis 22:1–14: in his last words Mattathias asks whether Abraham was not found faithful when tested, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Genesis tells of God testing Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac. Mattathias joins that test to the words Genesis uses of Abraham's faith, as the first of a line of ancestors he holds up to his sons.

ends.excerpt: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him…
Wasn’t Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness?

connections.label: Joseph became lord of Egypt
connections.explanation: 1 Maccabees 2:53 recalls Genesis 41:39–43: Joseph kept the commandment when he was in distress, and became lord of Egypt. Genesis tells how Pharaoh set Joseph over all Egypt after he interpreted the dreams. Mattathias names the reason he sees in the story, faithfulness under trial, as he urges his sons to keep the law.

ends.excerpt: Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Because God has shown you all of this, there is no one so discreet and wise as you.
Joseph in the time of his distress kept the commandment, and became lord of Egypt. Phinehas our father, because he was exceedingly zealous, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.

connections.label: Phinehas our father
connections.explanation: 1 Maccabees 2:54 recalls Numbers 25:7–13: Phinehas, for his zeal, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Numbers tells of Phinehas's spear at Peor and of the LORD's covenant of a lasting priesthood for his zeal. Mattathias, who has just killed an apostate at Modein in the same zeal, calls Phinehas our father.

ends.excerpt: When Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from the middle of the congregation, and took a spear in his hand.
Phinehas our father, because he was exceedingly zealous, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.

connections.label: Elijah, zealous for the law
connections.explanation: 1 Maccabees 2:58 recalls 2 Kings 2:11: Elijah was taken up into heaven for his zeal for the law. Kings tells of the chariot of fire and the whirlwind that took Elijah. Mattathias gives the reason in his own words, zeal, the virtue his whole speech commends.

ends.sectionTitle: Elijah's Last Acts; the Chariot of Fire
ends.excerpt: As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Elijah was taken up into heaven because he was exceedingly zealous for the law. Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael believed, and were saved out of the flame.

connections.label: Saved out of the flame
connections.explanation: 1 Maccabees 2:59 recalls Daniel 3:19–27: the three who believed, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, were saved from the fire. Daniel tells of the three young men thrown bound into the furnace, heated seven times more than usual, and coming out unharmed. Mattathias names them by their Hebrew names, as the book of Daniel does at its start.

ends.excerpt: Then Nebuchadnezzar was full of fury, and the form of his appearance was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more…
Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael believed, and were saved out of the flame. Daniel was delivered from the mouth of lions for his innocence.

connections.label: Delivered from the lions
connections.explanation: 1 Maccabees 2:60 recalls Daniel 6:16–22: Daniel was delivered from the mouth of lions for his innocence. Daniel tells of the night in the lions' den and of the angel God sent to shut their mouths, because Daniel was found innocent. Mattathias ends his list of the faithful there.

ends.excerpt: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, “Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.”
Daniel was delivered from the mouth of lions for his innocence. “Thus consider from generation to generation that no one who put their trust in him will lack for strength.

connections.label: The God of my father Simeon
connections.explanation: Judith 9:2–4 recalls Genesis 34:25–31: Judith prays to the God of her father Simeon, who gave him a sword to avenge his sister's defilement. Genesis tells how Simeon and Levi killed the men of Shechem after Dinah was taken, and how Jacob rebuked them. Judith, about to go out against Holofernes, praises the deed and asks for strength to act.

ends.excerpt: On the third day, when they were sore, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, each took his sword, came upon the unsuspecting city, and killed all the males.
“O Lord God of my father Simeon, into whose hand you gave a sword to take vengeance on the strangers who loosened the belt of a virgin to defile her, uncovered her thigh to her shame, and profaned…

connections.label: Remember how he tried the fathers
connections.explanation: Judith 8:26 recalls Genesis 22:1: Judith reminds the elders of all God did to Abraham and how he tried Isaac and Jacob. Genesis tells how God tested Abraham. Judith, rebuking the elders for setting God a deadline, says the trials of the ancestors were for their good, as the siege is for the town's.

ends.excerpt: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him…
Remember all the things which he did to Abraham, and all the things in which he tried Isaac, and all the things which happened to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria, when he kept the sheep of Laban his…

connections.label: The day before Mordecai's day
connections.explanation: 2 Maccabees 15:36 names the feast of Esther 9:20–22: the day of victory over Nicanor falls on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Mordecai's day. Esther tells how Mordecai wrote to the Jews to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as days of joy. Second Maccabees sets a new feast beside it and calls the older one by Mordecai's name.

ends.excerpt: Mordecai wrote these things in a book and sent them to the Jews, as many as were in the kingdom of Ahasuerus, both those who were near and those who were far away,
They all ordained with a common decree to in no way let this day pass undistinguished, but to mark with honor the thirteenth day of the twelfth month (it is called Adar in the Syrian language), the…

connections.label: Robed, mounted and proclaimed
connections.explanation: Genesis 41:42–43 and Esther 6:11 both tell of a Hebrew in a foreign court honoured by the king with royal clothing, a ride through the city and a herald crying out before him. Pharaoh dresses Joseph in fine linen, puts his ring on his hand and has him ride in the second chariot; the king has Haman robe Mordecai, mount him on the royal horse and proclaim his honour, and later gives Mordecai his ring. The words for clothing and riding are the same (below).

ends.excerpt: Pharaoh took off his signet ring from his hand, and put it on Joseph’s hand, and arrayed him in robes of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck.
So Haman took the robe and the horse, dressed Mordecai, mounted him on the horse, and went through the streets of the city, proclaiming, “This is what will be done for every man whom the king wishes…

connections.label: Job, among the righteous three
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 14:14 names Job of Job 1:1: Noah, Daniel and Job, even if all three were in a guilty land, would save only themselves. Job is introduced as blameless and upright, fearing God and turning from evil. Ezekiel counts him among three men known for their righteousness (the name below).

ends.excerpt: There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil.

ends.sectionTitle: The Exile Acted Out; False Prophets
ends.excerpt: though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness,” says the Lord GOD.

connections.label: What is man?
connections.explanation: Job 7:17–18 and Psalms 8:4 both tell of the question what man is, that God should take note of him. The psalm asks it in wonder at God's care for so small a creature; Job asks it in complaint, wishing God would stop visiting and testing him every moment. The verb for God's visiting is the same (below); which was written first is not stated.

ends.excerpt: What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him, that you should visit him every morning, and test him every moment?
what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him? For you have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor.

connections.label: Cursed be the day I was born
connections.explanation: Job 3:3–10 and Jeremiah 20:14–18 both tell of a man cursing the day he was born and the news of a boy's birth. Job, after his losses, wishes his day had never come and calls darkness down on it; Jeremiah, after a night in the stocks, curses the day and the man who brought his father the news. The words for cursing and for trouble are shared (below).

ends.excerpt: “Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.’
Cursed is the day in which I was born. Don’t let the day in which my mother bore me be blessed.

connections.label: The fear of the Lord
connections.explanation: Job 28:28 and Proverbs 1:7 both tell that the fear of the Lord is where wisdom begins. Job's poem on wisdom ends with God's word to humankind that the fear of the Lord is wisdom and turning from evil is understanding; Proverbs opens its collection with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge. The words for fear and for wisdom are the same (below).

ends.sectionTitle: Job's Oath; Where Wisdom Is Found
ends.excerpt: To man he said, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. To depart from evil is understanding.’”

ends.sectionTitle: Wisdom’s Call and a Father’s Warnings
ends.excerpt: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

connections.label: The LORD's hand has done this
connections.explanation: Job 12:9 and Isaiah 41:20 both tell, in the same words, that the LORD's hand has done this. Job says even the animals know that the LORD's hand made them. Isaiah says the nations will see the desert made green and know that the LORD's hand has done it.

ends.excerpt: Who doesn’t know that in all these, the LORD’s hand has done this, in whose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?

ends.sectionTitle: Comfort for the Exiles; the Servant
ends.excerpt: that they may see, know, consider, and understand together, that the LORD’s hand has done this, and the Holy One of Israel has created it.

connections.label: Naked from the womb
connections.explanation: Job 1:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:15 both tell that a person comes from his mother's womb naked and will go back naked. Job says it while blessing the LORD who gave and took away; the Preacher says it of the rich man who can carry nothing of his labour away in his hand. The words for naked and for the womb are the same (below).

ends.excerpt: He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the LORD’s name.”

ends.sectionTitle: Vows, Wealth and What Is Good
ends.excerpt: As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.

connections.label: Who measured the world?
connections.explanation: Job 38:4–11 and Isaiah 40:12 both tell of God's questions about who measured and laid out the world. The LORD asks Job where he was when the earth's foundations were laid and who stretched the measuring line on it. Isaiah asks who has measured the waters in his hand, marked off the sky and weighed the mountains in scales.

ends.excerpt: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Declare, if you have understanding.

ends.sectionTitle: Comfort for the Exiles; the Servant

connections.label: Micah quoted at Jeremiah's trial
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12: elders at Jeremiah's trial recall that Micah of Moresheth prophesied that Zion would be ploughed like a field. Micah's word, that Jerusalem would become heaps and the temple mount a wooded height, had been spoken in Hezekiah's day. The elders cite it to show that a prophet who foretold the temple's ruin was not put to death, and Jeremiah's life is spared (shared words below).

ends.excerpt: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.

“Micah the Morashtite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah; and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies says: “‘Zion will be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem will…

connections.label: Sour grapes
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 31:29–30 and Ezekiel 18:2–4 both tell of the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth set on edge, and of its end. Jeremiah promises days when it will no longer be said, for each will die for his own iniquity; Ezekiel has God forbid the proverb at once, since every soul is his. The rare words for sour grapes and for teeth set on edge are shared (below).

ends.excerpt: “In those days they will say no more, “‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’

ends.sectionTitle: The Eagles and the Cedar; Each Answers for His Own Sin
ends.excerpt: “What do you mean, that you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’?

connections.label: One oracle against Edom
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 49:14–16 and Obadiah 1:1–4 both tell the same oracle against Edom: news from the LORD, an envoy sent among the nations, and Edom brought down from its rocky heights. The verses run almost word for word, the pride of Edom's heart deceiving those who live in the clefts of the rock (shared words below). Which prophet's words came first is not stated.

ends.excerpt: I have heard news from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the nations, saying, “Gather yourselves together! Come against her! Rise up to the battle!”
The vision of Obadiah. This is what the Lord GOD says about Edom. We have heard news from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the nations, saying, “Arise, and let’s rise up against her in…

connections.label: Though Moses and Samuel stood before me
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 15:1 names Moses of Exodus 32:11–14: even if Moses and Samuel stood before the LORD, he would not turn toward this people. Exodus tells how Moses pleaded for Israel after the golden calf and the LORD relented. Jeremiah hears that the time for such pleading has passed, naming the two great intercessors to say so.

ends.excerpt: Moses begged the LORD his God, and said, “LORD, why does your wrath burn hot against your people, that you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?
Then the LORD said to me, “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind would not turn toward this people. Cast them out of my sight, and let them go out!

connections.label: Rachel weeping for her children
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 31:15 names Rachel of Genesis 35:16–20: a voice is heard in Ramah, Rachel weeping for her children. Genesis tells how Rachel died giving birth on the road to Ephrath and was buried there. Jeremiah hears her weeping for children taken away, before God promises that they will return (the name below).

ends.excerpt: They traveled from Bethel. There was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and Rachel travailed. She had hard labor.
The LORD says: “A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children. She refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more.”

connections.label: The clay and the potter
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 18:1–6 and Isaiah 64:8 both tell of God as the potter and his people as the clay. Jeremiah watches a potter remake a spoiled vessel and hears that Israel is in God's hand as clay in the potter's. Isaiah's lament turns the image into a plea from the clay to its maker, with the same words for clay and potter (below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Potter and the Broken Jar
ends.excerpt: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying, “Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause you to hear my words.”
But now, LORD, you are our Father. We are the clay and you our potter. We all are the work of your hand.

connections.label: The Branch
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 23:5–6 and Zechariah 6:12 both tell of a man called the Branch, raised up for David's line. Jeremiah promises a righteous Branch for David who will reign wisely and whose name will be the LORD our righteousness; Zechariah is told to crown the man whose name is the Branch, who will build the LORD's temple. The word for the Branch is the same (below).

ends.excerpt: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will raise to David a righteous Branch; and he will reign as king and deal wisely, and will execute justice and righteousness in the land.
and speak to him, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies says, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch! He will grow up out of his place; and he will build the LORD’s temple.

connections.label: The throne of fire
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 1:26–28 and Daniel 7:9–10 both tell of a vision of God enthroned, with fire, wheels and a figure on the throne. Ezekiel sees the likeness of a throne above the living creatures, with one like a man on it, wrapped in fire and brightness. Daniel sees the Ancient of Days take his seat, his throne flames of fire with wheels of burning fire and a stream of fire flowing from it.

ends.sectionTitle: The Vision of God’s Glory; the Prophet’s Call
ends.excerpt: Above the expanse that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone. On the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a man on it above.

ends.sectionTitle: Four Beasts and the Son of Man
ends.excerpt: “I watched until thrones were placed, and one who was Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning…

connections.label: Those who sleep in the dust will awake
connections.explanation: Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2 both tell of those who lie in the dust awaking. Isaiah promises that God's dead will live and those who dwell in the dust will wake and sing; Daniel says many asleep in the earth's dust will wake, some to everlasting life and some to shame. The words for awaking and for the dust are the same (below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Earth Judged; a Feast on the Mountain
ends.excerpt: Your dead shall live. Their dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

connections.label: Who knows? He may turn and relent
connections.explanation: Joel 2:13–14 and Jonah 3:9–4:2 both tell of a God gracious and merciful who may turn and relent of the disaster, and both ask who knows. Joel calls Judah to tear their hearts and return, for perhaps God will leave a blessing; in Jonah the king of Nineveh hopes the same, God relents, and Jonah complains with the same confession Joel makes (below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Locusts and a Call to Mourn
ends.excerpt: Tear your heart and not your garments, and turn to the LORD, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.
Who knows whether God will not turn and relent, and turn away from his fierce anger, so that we might not perish?”

connections.label: All your waves and billows
connections.explanation: Psalms 42:7 and Jonah 2:3 both tell the same line: all your waves and your billows have gone over me. In the psalm the waters are the singer's despair far from the temple; in Jonah they are the sea itself, into which he was thrown. The words for the breakers and the waves are the same (below).

ends.excerpt: Deep calls to deep at the noise of your waterfalls. All your waves and your billows have swept over me.

ends.sectionTitle: In the Belly of the Fish
ends.excerpt: For you threw me into the depths, in the heart of the seas. The flood was all around me. All your waves and your billows passed over me.

connections.label: If that nation turns from its evil
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 18:7–8 and Jonah 3:10 both tell of God relenting of the disaster he had spoken against a nation that turns from its evil. Jeremiah states it as a rule at the potter's house; Jonah shows it happening to Nineveh, a foreign city, when its people turn from their evil ways. The verb for relenting is the same (below).

ends.sectionTitle: The Potter and the Broken Jar
ends.excerpt: At the instant I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy it,
God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way. God relented of the disaster which he said he would do to them, and he didn’t do it.

connections.label: Swords into ploughshares
connections.explanation: Isaiah 2:2–4 and Micah 4:1–3 both tell of the mountain of the LORD's house raised above the hills, the nations streaming to it to learn his ways, and swords beaten into ploughshares. The two passages run nearly word for word. Micah adds that each will sit under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to make them afraid.

ends.excerpt: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it.

ends.sectionTitle: The Mountain of the Lord; a Ruler from Bethlehem
ends.excerpt: But in the latter days, it will happen that the mountain of the LORD’s temple will be established on the top of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills; and peoples will stream to it.

connections.label: Ploughshares into swords
connections.explanation: Isaiah 2:4 is set against Joel 3:10: where Isaiah sees the nations beating swords into ploughshares, Joel summons them to beat ploughshares into swords. Joel's call is to the valley of judgement, where the LORD will judge the surrounding nations. The same image runs both ways.

ends.excerpt: He will judge between the nations, and will decide concerning many peoples. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against…

ends.sectionTitle: Judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat
ends.excerpt: Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weak say, ‘I am strong.’

connections.label: The LORD roars from Zion
connections.explanation: Joel 3:16 and Amos 1:2 both tell that the LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem. Joel follows it with heaven and earth shaking and the LORD a refuge for his people; Amos opens his book with it, the shepherds' pastures mourning and the top of Carmel withering.

ends.sectionTitle: Judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat
ends.excerpt: The LORD will roar from Zion, and thunder from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth will shake; but the LORD will be a refuge to his people, and a stronghold to the children of Israel.
He said: “The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the pastures of the shepherds will mourn, and the top of Carmel will wither.”

connections.label: The mountains drip sweet wine
connections.explanation: Joel 3:18 and Amos 9:13 both tell of a coming day when the mountains will drip with sweet wine. Joel adds the hills flowing with milk and a fountain from the LORD's house; Amos adds the ploughman overtaking the reaper as Israel's fortunes are restored.

ends.sectionTitle: Judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat
ends.excerpt: It will happen in that day, that the mountains will drop down sweet wine, the hills will flow with milk, all the brooks of Judah will flow with waters; and a fountain will flow out from the LORD’s…
