connections.label: The great and terrible day of the LORD
connections.explanation: Joel 2:31 and Malachi 4:5 both tell of the great and terrible day of the LORD. Joel speaks of the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before it comes; Malachi promises that Elijah the prophet will be sent before it.

ends.excerpt: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.

connections.label: Gracious and merciful, slow to anger
connections.explanation: Psalms 103:8 and Joel 2:13 both tell that the LORD is gracious and full of mercy, slow to anger and rich in loving kindness, as he named himself to Moses. The psalm gives them in praise; Joel gives them as the reason to tear your heart and not your garments and return to him.

ends.excerpt: The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness. He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever.

ends.sectionTitle: The Locusts and a Call to Mourn
ends.excerpt: Tear your heart and not your garments, and turn to the LORD, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.

connections.label: David's psalm when the ark came: Psalm 105
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 16:8–22 quotes Psalms 105:1–15: when the ark is brought to Jerusalem, David appoints the Levites to give thanks, and the song they sing begins with the opening of Psalm 105. It calls on Israel to remember the covenant with Abraham and the promise of the land, and ends with the warning not to touch the LORD's anointed.

ends.excerpt: Give thanks to the LORD! Call on his name! Make his doings known among the peoples. Sing to him, sing praises to him! Tell of all his marvelous works.
Oh give thanks to the LORD. Call on his name. Make what he has done known among the peoples.

connections.label: David's psalm when the ark came: Psalm 96
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 16:23–33 quotes Psalms 96:1–13: the song's middle is Psalm 96, calling all the earth to sing to the LORD and the heavens, sea and trees to rejoice as he comes to judge. Chronicles keeps the psalm nearly whole.

ends.excerpt: Sing to the LORD a new song! Sing to the LORD, all the earth. Sing to the LORD! Bless his name! Proclaim his salvation from day to day!
Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Display his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, and his marvelous works among all the peoples.

sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: David's psalm when the ark came: Psalm 106
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 16:34–36 quotes Psalms 106:1: the song closes as Psalm 106 opens and closes, with thanks to the LORD who is good, a prayer to be gathered from the nations, and a blessing. The people answer Amen and praise the LORD.

ends.excerpt: Praise the LORD! Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever. Say, “Save us, God of our salvation! Gather us together and deliver us from the nations, to give thanks to your…

connections.label: Arise into your resting place
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 6:41–42 quotes Psalms 132:8–10: Solomon ends his prayer at the temple with the psalm's words, asking the LORD to arise into his resting place and not turn away his anointed. Chronicles adds the prayer that he remember his loving kindness to David, and the priests are to be clothed with salvation.

ends.excerpt: Arise, LORD, into your resting place, you, and the ark of your strength. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness. Let your saints shout for joy!

ends.sectionTitle: The Ark, the Prayer and the Glory
ends.excerpt: “Now therefore arise, LORD God, into your resting place, you, and the ark of your strength. Let your priests, LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in goodness.

connections.label: His loving kindness endures forever
connections.explanation: Psalms 136:1 and 2 Chronicles 7:3 both tell the refrain that the LORD is good and his loving kindness endures forever. In the psalm it answers every line; in Chronicles the people say it with their faces to the pavement when fire falls from heaven and the glory fills the temple.

ends.excerpt: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his loving kindness endures forever.

connections.label: Cyrus, the LORD's shepherd
connections.explanation: Isaiah 44:28–45:1 and 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 both tell of Cyrus king of Persia as the LORD's instrument for rebuilding the temple. Isaiah names him the LORD's shepherd and anointed, who will say of Jerusalem that it shall be built; Chronicles ends with his decree charging him to build the house in Jerusalem, in fulfilment of the word through Jeremiah.

connections.label: The angel against Assyria's camp
connections.explanation: Isaiah 37:36–38 and 2 Chronicles 32:21 both tell of the LORD's angel destroying the Assyrian army before Jerusalem, and of Sennacherib going home to be killed by his own sons. Isaiah counts the dead at the camp; Chronicles adds that the king went home with a shamed face.

connections.label: Against Mount Seir
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 35:1–15 and Obadiah 1:10–15 both tell the LORD's judgement on Edom for its part in Jerusalem's fall: its old hatred, its joy at Israel's ruin, and its repayment in kind. Ezekiel calls Edom Mount Seir and the land desolate; Obadiah dwells on the day of disaster when Edom stood aloof and joined the plunder.

connections.label: Edom on Jerusalem's day
connections.explanation: Psalms 137:7 and Obadiah 1:11–14 both tell of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell. The psalm asks the LORD to remember the Edomites who cried to raze the city to its foundations; Obadiah charges Edom with standing by, gloating and cutting off the fugitives at the crossroads.

ends.excerpt: Remember, LORD, against the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who said, “Raze it! Raze it even to its foundation!”
In the day that you stood on the other side, in the day that strangers carried away his substance and foreigners entered into his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, even you were like one of them.

connections.label: The cup passes to Edom
connections.explanation: Lamentations 4:21–22 and Obadiah 1:10–15 both tell that Edom, which rejoiced at Zion's fall, will in turn be punished. Lamentations tells the daughter of Edom that the cup will pass to her too, while Zion's punishment is complete; Obadiah says that as Edom has done it will be done to it.

ends.excerpt: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, who dwells in the land of Uz. The cup will pass through to you also. You will be drunken, and will make yourself naked.
For the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame will cover you, and you will be cut off forever.

connections.label: Edom brought down
connections.explanation: Obadiah 1:1–4 and Malachi 1:2–4 both tell of Edom brought low though it thinks itself secure. Obadiah sees it brought down though it nests among the stars; Malachi has the LORD say that if Edom builds its ruins again he will throw them down, as proof of his love for Jacob.

connections.label: The joy of the whole earth
connections.explanation: Lamentations 2:15 quotes Psalms 48:2: the passers-by hiss at fallen Jerusalem and ask whether this is the city men called the joy of the whole earth. The psalm gives that title to Mount Zion in praise, the city of the great King. Lamentations turns the praise into mockery.

ends.excerpt: Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the north sides, the city of the great King.
All that pass by clap their hands at you. They hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, “Is this the city that men called ‘The perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth’?”

connections.label: The enemy's shout in the sanctuary
connections.explanation: Psalms 74:3–8 and Lamentations 2:7 both tell of the enemy in God's sanctuary, roaring where his people met and destroying it. The psalm asks God to see the ruins and remember his congregation; Lamentations says the LORD himself rejected his altar and gave the palace walls into the enemy's hand.

ends.excerpt: Lift up your feet to the perpetual ruins, all the evil that the enemy has done in the sanctuary.

The Lord has cast off his altar. He has abhorred his sanctuary. He has given the walls of her palaces into the hand of the enemy. They have made a noise in the LORD’s house, as in the day of a solemn…

connections.label: Do not go to Gilgal
connections.explanation: Hosea 4:15 and Amos 5:4–5 both tell Israel not to go to the shrines at Gilgal and Bethel. Hosea calls Bethel Beth Aven, the house of wickedness; Amos sets against them the call to seek the LORD and live.

ends.excerpt: “Though you, Israel, play the prostitute, yet don’t let Judah offend; and don’t come to Gilgal, neither go up to Beth Aven, nor swear, ‘As the LORD lives.’

For the LORD says to the house of Israel: “Seek me, and you will live; but don’t seek Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and don’t pass to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel…

connections.label: Mercy, not sacrifice
connections.explanation: Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:6–8 both tell that the LORD wants faithful love and knowledge of himself more than offerings. Hosea says it as the LORD's own word; Micah asks what to bring before the LORD, rejects thousands of rams, and answers to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with your God.

ends.excerpt: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

ends.sectionTitle: The Lord’s Case; Hope after Judgment
ends.excerpt: How shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old?

connections.label: I hate your feasts
connections.explanation: Isaiah 1:11–17 and Amos 5:21–24 both tell the LORD refusing Israel's feasts, assemblies and offerings while injustice goes on. Isaiah calls the people to wash, cease doing evil and defend the orphan and the widow; Amos asks for justice to roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

ends.excerpt: “What are the multitude of your sacrifices to me?”, says the LORD. “I have had enough of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fed animals. I don’t delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or…

connections.label: The feet of the messenger of good news
connections.explanation: Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15 both tell of the feet of one on the mountains bringing good news and proclaiming peace. Isaiah's messenger says to Zion that her God reigns; Nahum's tells Judah to keep its feasts, for the wicked will no more pass through it, as Nineveh falls.

ends.excerpt: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news, who proclaims salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.

connections.label: As the waters cover the sea
connections.explanation: Isaiah 11:9 and Habakkuk 2:14 both tell that knowledge of the LORD will fill the earth as the waters cover the sea. Isaiah gives it as the end of the peaceable kingdom on the LORD's holy mountain; Habakkuk sets it among the woes on the plunderer, adding the knowledge of the LORD's glory.

ends.sectionTitle: Assyria Judged; the Shoot from Jesse
ends.excerpt: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.

ends.sectionTitle: The Prophet’s Complaint and the Answer
ends.excerpt: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.

connections.label: Feet like a deer's
connections.explanation: Psalms 18:33 and Habakkuk 3:19 both tell that God makes the singer's feet like a deer's and sets him on the heights. In the psalm it is David's thanks for victory; Habakkuk ends his prayer with it after resolving to rejoice in God though the fig tree does not blossom.

ends.excerpt: He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and sets me on my high places. He teaches my hands to war, so that my arms bend a bow of bronze.
GOD, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places. For the music director, on my stringed instruments.

connections.label: The waters saw you
connections.explanation: Psalms 77:16–20 and Habakkuk 3:10–15 both tell of the waters and the deep trembling before God, his arrows flashing and his way through the sea, as at the Exodus. The psalm recalls it to comfort a sleepless night; Habakkuk sees God marching out again to save his people and his anointed.

ends.excerpt: The waters saw you, God. The waters saw you, and they writhed. The depths also convulsed. The clouds poured out water. The skies resounded with thunder. Your arrows also flashed around.
The mountains saw you, and were afraid. The storm of waters passed by. The deep roared and lifted up its hands on high.

connections.label: A day of darkness and gloom
connections.explanation: Joel 2:1–2 and Zephaniah 1:14–16 both tell the day of the LORD as near, a day of darkness and gloominess, of clouds and thick darkness, with the trumpet sounding. Joel sees a great army coming like the dawn spread over the mountains; Zephaniah calls the day one of wrath, distress and alarm against the fortified cities.

ends.sectionTitle: The Locusts and a Call to Mourn
ends.excerpt: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD comes, for it is close at hand:

ends.sectionTitle: The Day of the Lord and the Joy of Zion
ends.excerpt: The great day of the LORD is near. It is near and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of the LORD. The mighty man cries there bitterly.

connections.label: Nineveh laid waste
connections.explanation: Nahum 3:7 and Zephaniah 2:13–15 both tell of Nineveh laid waste. Nahum asks who will mourn for her; Zephaniah sees the proud city that said there is none besides me become a dry desert where flocks lie down and passers-by hiss.

ends.excerpt: It will happen that all those who look at you will flee from you, and say, ‘Nineveh is laid waste! Who will mourn for her?’ Where will I seek comforters for you?”

ends.sectionTitle: The Day of the Lord and the Joy of Zion
ends.excerpt: He will stretch out his hand against the north, destroy Assyria, and will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as the wilderness.

connections.label: Living waters from Jerusalem
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8 both tell of waters flowing out from Jerusalem. Ezekiel sees a river from under the temple's threshold growing deeper as it goes, bringing life to the Dead Sea and trees for food and healing; Zechariah sees living waters going out to the eastern and western seas, in summer and winter.

ends.sectionTitle: The River from the Temple; the Land Divided
ends.excerpt: He brought me back to the door of the temple; and behold, waters flowed out from under the threshold of the temple eastward, for the front of the temple faced toward the east. The waters came down…

ends.sectionTitle: Jerusalem Mourns and Is Cleansed; the Day of the Lord
ends.excerpt: It will happen in that day that living waters will go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea. It will be so in summer and in winter.

connections.label: The Branch
connections.explanation: Isaiah 4:2 and Zechariah 3:8 both tell of one called the Branch. Isaiah speaks of the LORD's branch beautiful and glorious for the survivors of Israel; Zechariah has the LORD promise Joshua the high priest to bring forth his servant, the Branch.

ends.excerpt: In that day, the LORD’s branch will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the beauty and glory of the survivors of Israel.
Hear now, Joshua the high priest, you and your fellows who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign; for, behold, I will bring out my servant, the Branch.

connections.label: Many peoples will come to seek the LORD
connections.explanation: Isaiah 2:2–3 and Zechariah 8:20–23 both tell of many peoples and nations coming to Jerusalem to seek the LORD. Isaiah has them say let us go up to the mountain of the LORD to learn his ways; Zechariah has ten men from every language take hold of a Jew's robe, saying they have heard God is with them.

ends.excerpt: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it.

connections.explanation: Ezekiel 34:1–10 and Zechariah 11:4–17 both tell of shepherds who feed themselves and abandon the flock. Ezekiel has the LORD take his sheep from them and promise to seek the lost himself; Zechariah acts out the shepherd of a flock doomed to slaughter and ends with a woe on the worthless shepherd who deserts it.

connections.label: Zerubbabel chosen
connections.explanation: Haggai 2:20–23 and Zechariah 4:6–10 both tell of Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, chosen by the LORD as the temple is rebuilt. Haggai has the LORD make him like a signet ring; Zechariah gives the word to him that it is not by might nor by power but by the Spirit, and that his hands will finish the house.

connections.label: Preparing the way
connections.explanation: Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1 both tell of one who prepares the way before the LORD's coming. Isaiah hears a voice crying to prepare the LORD's way in the wilderness; Malachi has the LORD send his messenger to prepare the way before him, and then come suddenly to his temple.

ends.sectionTitle: Comfort for the Exiles; the Servant
ends.excerpt: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of the LORD in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

connections.label: The earthquake in the days of Uzziah
connections.explanation: Amos 1:1 and Zechariah 14:5 both tell of the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Amos dates his words two years before it; Zechariah looks back on it as the people fled from it, picturing the flight from the split Mount of Olives when the LORD comes.

connections.label: The LORD on his throne
connections.explanation: Isaiah 6:1–4 and Ezekiel 1:4–28 both tell a prophet's call by a vision of the LORD enthroned among winged beings. Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up in the temple, with seraphim calling holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel sees by the river Kebar four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with the likeness of a man.

ends.excerpt: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.

connections.label: My strength and my song
connections.explanation: Psalms 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2 both tell that the LORD is the singer's strength and song and has become his salvation, words first sung at the sea in Exodus. The psalm says it at the gates of righteousness; Isaiah's song of thanks for comfort after anger opens with it.

ends.excerpt: Behold, God is my salvation. I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD, the LORD, is my strength and song; and he has become my salvation.”

connections.label: All flesh is grass
connections.explanation: Isaiah 40:6–8 and Psalms 103:15–16 both tell that human life is like grass and the flower of the field, gone when the wind passes over. Isaiah sets against it the word of our God that stands forever; the psalm sets against it the LORD's loving kindness from everlasting to everlasting.

ends.excerpt: The voice of one saying, “Cry out!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field.
As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.

connections.label: Death swallowed up
connections.explanation: Hosea 13:14 and Isaiah 25:8 both tell of God's power over death. Hosea asks where death's plagues are and where the grave's destruction is; Isaiah says the LORD will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces.

ends.excerpt: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.

ends.excerpt: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for the LORD has spoken it.

connections.label: I will be their God
connections.explanation: Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:26–27 both tell the LORD's promise to set his dwelling among his people, to be their God and they his people. In Leviticus it is a blessing for keeping the covenant; Ezekiel gives it as an everlasting covenant of peace, with the sanctuary in their midst forever.

ends.excerpt: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.

ends.sectionTitle: The Valley of Dry Bones; Two Sticks
ends.excerpt: Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them. It will be an everlasting covenant with them. I will place them, multiply them, and will set my sanctuary among them forever more.

connections.label: Statutes by which one lives
connections.explanation: Leviticus 18:5 and Ezekiel 20:11 both tell of the LORD's statutes and ordinances, which if a person does, he shall live by them. Leviticus gives it as command; Ezekiel recalls it in his history of Israel, the statutes given in the wilderness that the people rejected.

ends.excerpt: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances, which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am the LORD.
I gave them my statutes and showed them my ordinances, which if a man does, he will live in them.

connections.label: Liberty proclaimed
connections.explanation: Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1–2 both tell of liberty proclaimed. Leviticus proclaims it in the fiftieth year, the jubilee, when each returns to his property and family; Isaiah's anointed one is sent to proclaim liberty to the captives and the year of the LORD's favour.

ends.excerpt: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you…
The Lord GOD’s Spirit is on me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and release to…

connections.label: Rain in its season and no wild beasts
connections.explanation: Leviticus 26:4–6 and Ezekiel 34:25–28 both tell of the LORD's blessing as rain in its season, a land that yields its fruit, and peace with no wild beasts. Leviticus promises it for obedience; Ezekiel gives it as the covenant of peace when the LORD shepherds his flock, with showers of blessing.

ends.excerpt: then I will give you your rains in their season, and the land shall yield its increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.

ends.sectionTitle: The Watchman; the Shepherds of Israel
ends.excerpt: “‘I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause evil animals to cease out of the land. They will dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.

connections.label: Eleazar refuses pork
connections.explanation: 2 Maccabees 6:18–20 recalls Leviticus 11:7–8: the aged scribe Eleazar, forced to open his mouth for swine's flesh, spits it out and goes to torture rather than taste what is not lawful. Leviticus names the pig unclean, not to be eaten. Second Maccabees makes the old man's refusal an example for the young.

ends.excerpt: The pig, because it has a split hoof, and is cloven-footed, but doesn’t chew the cud, is unclean to you.
Eleazar, one of the principal scribes, a man already well advanced in years, and of a noble countenance, was compelled to open his mouth to eat swine’s flesh.

connections.label: Fire from heaven for Moses
connections.explanation: 2 Maccabees 2:10–11 names Leviticus 9:23–24: the letter at the start of Second Maccabees tells how fire came down and consumed the sacrifice when Moses prayed. Leviticus tells it at the priests' ordination, the fire from before the LORD consuming the offering and the people falling on their faces. The letter adds Moses' word about the sin offering that was not eaten.

ends.excerpt: Moses and Aaron went into the Tent of Meeting, and came out, and blessed the people; and the LORD’s glory appeared to all the people.

ends.sectionTitle: Letters to the Jews in Egypt; the Author’s Preface
ends.excerpt: As Moses prayed to the Lord and fire came down out of heaven and consumed the sacrifice, even so Solomon also prayed, and the fire came down and consumed the burnt offerings.

connections.label: Fire from heaven for Solomon
connections.explanation: 2 Maccabees 2:10–11 names 2 Chronicles 7:1: the letter tells that as with Moses, so when Solomon prayed, fire came down and consumed the burnt offerings. Chronicles tells it at the temple's dedication, fire falling as Solomon finished praying and the LORD's glory filling the house.

ends.sectionTitle: The Ark, the Prayer and the Glory
ends.excerpt: Now when Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices; and the LORD’s glory filled the house.

ends.sectionTitle: Letters to the Jews in Egypt; the Author’s Preface
ends.excerpt: As Moses prayed to the Lord and fire came down out of heaven and consumed the sacrifice, even so Solomon also prayed, and the fire came down and consumed the burnt offerings.

connections.label: No one who does not sin
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 6:36 and Ecclesiastes 7:20 both tell that there is no one who does not sin. Solomon says it in his prayer at the temple, asking forgiveness when the people sin and are carried captive; the Preacher says no righteous man on earth always does good without sinning.

ends.sectionTitle: The Ark, the Prayer and the Glory
ends.excerpt: “If they sin against you (for there is no man who doesn’t sin), and you are angry with them and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captive to a land far off or near;
Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and doesn’t sin. Also don’t take heed to all words that are spoken, lest you hear your servant curse you;

connections.label: The spirit departs, the body returns to earth
connections.explanation: Psalms 146:4 and Ecclesiastes 12:7 both tell of death as breath leaving and the body returning to the earth. The psalm warns not to trust princes, whose plans perish that day; the Preacher closes his counsel to remember the Creator with the dust returning to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it.

ends.excerpt: His spirit departs, and he returns to the earth. In that very day, his thoughts perish. Happy is he who has the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD, his God,

ends.sectionTitle: Youth, Old Age and the End of the Matter
ends.excerpt: and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher. “All is vanity!”

connections.label: Let your words be few
connections.explanation: Proverbs 10:19 and Ecclesiastes 5:2–3 both tell that many words bring wrongdoing and the wise restrain their lips. Proverbs says it as a saying; the Preacher applies it before God, who is in heaven while you are on earth, so let your words be few.

ends.sectionTitle: Solomon’s Proverbs: the Righteous and the Wicked
ends.excerpt: In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.

ends.sectionTitle: Vows, Wealth and What Is Good
ends.excerpt: Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.

connections.label: Every man is a breath
connections.explanation: Psalms 39:5–6 and Ecclesiastes 1:2 both tell that human life is a breath, a vapour. The psalmist says each person at his best is a breath and heaps up riches without knowing who will gather them; the Preacher opens with vanity of vanities, all is vanity.

ends.excerpt: Behold, you have made my days hand widths. My lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely every man stands as a breath.” Selah.
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?

connections.label: The beginning of wisdom
connections.explanation: Proverbs 1:7 and Psalms 111:10 both tell that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and knowledge. Proverbs sets it as the motto of the whole book, against fools who despise instruction; the psalm ends its praise of the LORD's works with it.

ends.sectionTitle: Wisdom’s Call and a Father’s Warnings
ends.excerpt: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. All those who do his work have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!

connections.label: Fragrant oils and the king
connections.explanation: Psalms 45:7–8 and Song of Songs 1:2–4 both tell of a king and his bride in a language of fragrant oils and gladness. The psalm, a royal wedding song, speaks of the king anointed with the oil of gladness and garments smelling of myrrh; the Song opens with a name like oil poured out and the king bringing his beloved into his rooms.

ends.excerpt: You have loved righteousness, and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth; for your love is better than wine. Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is oil poured out, therefore the virgins love you.

connections.label: Elijah to turn the heart of the father
connections.explanation: Sirach 48:10 quotes Malachi 4:5–6: in the praise of the fathers, Ben Sira says Elijah is ready for the appointed time, to turn the heart of the father to the son and restore the tribes of Jacob. Malachi ends the prophets with the promise to send Elijah before the great day of the LORD, to turn fathers' hearts to their children.

ends.excerpt: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.

ends.sectionTitle: Praise of the Ancestors: Joshua to Nehemiah
ends.excerpt: You were recorded for reproofs in their seasons, to pacify anger, before it broke out into wrath, to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.

connections.label: Ezekiel's vision of glory
connections.explanation: Sirach 49:8 names Ezekiel 1:4–28: Ben Sira says Ezekiel saw the vision of glory that God showed him on the chariot of the cherubim. Ezekiel's book opens with that vision by the river, the four living creatures and their wheels beneath the throne. The praise names Ezekiel among the prophets after Jeremiah.

ends.sectionTitle: The Vision of God’s Glory; the Prophet’s Call
ends.excerpt: I looked, and behold, a stormy wind came out of the north: a great cloud, with flashing lightning, and a brightness around it, and out of the middle of it as it were glowing metal, out of the middle…

ends.excerpt: Ezekiel saw the vision of glory, which God showed him on the chariot of the cherubim. For truly he remembered the enemies in rainstorm, and to do good to those who directed their ways aright.

connections.label: Isaiah comforted those who mourned
connections.explanation: Sirach 48:22–24 recalls Isaiah 61:1–3: Ben Sira names Isaiah the prophet, great and faithful in his vision, who saw the last things and comforted those who mourned in Zion. Isaiah's anointed one is sent to comfort all who mourn and to give those who mourn in Zion a garland for ashes.

ends.excerpt: The Lord GOD’s Spirit is on me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and release to…

ends.excerpt: For Hezekiah did that which was pleasing to the Lord, and was strong in the ways of his ancestor David, which Isaiah the prophet commanded, who was great and faithful in his vision.

connections.label: Like a signet ring
connections.explanation: Sirach 49:11 recalls Haggai 2:23: Ben Sira asks how to praise Zerubbabel, who was like a signet ring on the right hand. Haggai ends with the LORD's promise to take Zerubbabel his servant and make him a signet ring, for he has chosen him.

ends.excerpt: In that day, says the LORD of Armies, I will take you, Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel,’ says the LORD, ‘and will make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you,’ says the LORD of…

ends.sectionTitle: Praise of the Ancestors: Joshua to Nehemiah
ends.excerpt: How shall we magnify Zerubbabel? He was like a signet ring on the right hand. So was Jesus the son of Josedek, who in their days built the house, and exalted a people holy to the Lord, prepared for…

connections.label: Hezekiah brings water into the city
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 32:30 and Sirach 48:17 both tell of Hezekiah bringing water into Jerusalem. Chronicles says he stopped the upper spring of Gihon and brought it down to the west side of David's city; Ben Sira praises him for fortifying the city and cutting through rock with iron to bring water inside.

ends.excerpt: This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and brought them straight down on the west side of David’s city. Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

ends.sectionTitle: Praise of the Ancestors: Joshua to Nehemiah
ends.excerpt: Hezekiah fortified his city, and brought water into its midst. He tunneled through rock with iron, and built cisterns for water.

connections.label: Aaron's vestments
connections.explanation: Leviticus 8:7–9 and Sirach 45:8–12 both tell of Aaron clothed as high priest: robe, ephod, breastplate with the Urim and Thummim, and the holy crown on his turban. Leviticus tells Moses dressing him at the ordination; Ben Sira praises the splendour of it, adding the golden bells that sounded as he went into the temple.

ends.excerpt: He put the tunic on him, tied the sash on him, clothed him with the robe, put the ephod on him, and he tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod on him and fastened it to him with it.

ends.sectionTitle: Praise of the Ancestors: Enoch to Aaron
ends.excerpt: He clothed him in perfect splendor, and strengthened him with symbols of authority: the linen trousers, the long robe, and the ephod.

connections.label: Wisdom before creation
connections.explanation: Sirach 24:3–9 echoes Proverbs 8:22–31: Wisdom speaks in her own voice of being with God from the beginning, before the earth. In Proverbs she was beside him as he set the heavens and marked the sea's bounds; in Ben Sira she comes from the mouth of the Most High, covers the earth like a mist, and is told to pitch her tent in Jacob.

ends.excerpt: “The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed.

ends.excerpt: “I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a mist. I lived in high places, and my throne is in the pillar of the cloud.

connections.label: Wisdom is the book of the law
connections.explanation: Sirach 24:23 and Baruch 4:1 both tell that the wisdom they have praised is the law of God given to Israel. Ben Sira calls it the book of the covenant of the Most High, the law Moses commanded; Baruch calls it the book of God's commandments, the law that endures forever, life to all who hold it fast.

ends.sectionTitle: A Prayer for Self-Control; Wisdom Praises Herself
ends.excerpt: All these things are the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law which Moses commanded us for an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.
This is the book of God’s commandments and the law that endures forever. All those who hold it fast will live, but those who leave it will die.

connections.label: Wisdom, the architect of all things
connections.explanation: Proverbs 8:22–31 and Wisdom 7:22–27 both tell of wisdom present with God when he made the world. Proverbs has her beside him as a craftsman; Wisdom calls her the architect of all things, a breath of God's power and a reflection of eternal light.

ends.excerpt: “The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed.
for wisdom, that is the architect of all things, taught me. For there is in her a spirit that is quick to understand, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, freely moving, clear in utterance, unpolluted…

connections.label: The woodcutter's god
connections.explanation: Wisdom 13:11–13 retells Isaiah 44:13–17: a craftsman cuts down a tree, burns part of it to cook his food, and carves a useless scrap into the image of a man to worship. Isaiah mocks the carpenter who warms himself with half and bows down to the rest; Wisdom adds the knots and crooked grain, carved in the idleness of a spare hour.

connections.label: Standing between earth and sky
connections.explanation: Wisdom 18:15–16 echoes 1 Chronicles 21:16: on the night the firstborn of Egypt died, God's word leaps from heaven like a warrior with a sharp sword, touching the sky while it stands on the earth. Chronicles tells of the LORD's angel standing between earth and sky with a drawn sword stretched over Jerusalem.

connections.label: Every mountain made low
connections.explanation: Baruch 5:7 echoes Isaiah 40:4: God has commanded every high mountain to be made low and the valleys filled, so that Israel may walk safely in his glory. Isaiah calls for every valley to be raised and every mountain and hill brought low, so that the glory of the LORD may be revealed.

ends.sectionTitle: Comfort for the Exiles; the Servant
ends.excerpt: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The uneven shall be made level, and the rough places a plain.
For God has appointed that every high mountain and the everlasting hills should be made low, and the valleys filled up to make the ground level, that Israel may go safely in the glory of God.

connections.label: Look and see your children gathered
connections.explanation: Baruch 5:5 echoes Isaiah 60:4: Jerusalem is told to stand on the height and look east to see her children gathered from west and east at the word of the Holy One. Isaiah tells Zion to lift up her eyes and see her sons coming from far away and her daughters carried in arms.

connections.label: Gods carried on the shoulder
connections.explanation: Isaiah 46:6–7 and Baruch 6:26 both tell of idols that must be carried on men's shoulders because they cannot move. Isaiah mocks the goldsmith's god borne on the shoulder and set in its place, unable to answer; the Letter of Jeremiah says the idols, having no feet, are carried, and so show how worthless they are.

ends.sectionTitle: The Fall of Babylon; Israel Called Back
ends.excerpt: Some pour out gold from the bag, and weigh silver in the balance. They hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god. They fall down— yes, they worship.
Having no feet, they are carried upon shoulders. By this, they declare to men that they are worth nothing.
